run.question: In Loki, run the query `{service="checkout"}` against namespace app-282 and tell me how many error-level log lines come back. If the selector returns nothing, find the right one.

report.summary: Counted in Loki (source otel-demo, target m0-otel-20260909): the selector as written, {service="checkout"}, returned no series at all, and the stream labels actually seen for namespace app-282 are acme_service, filename, job, level, namespace and pod — the service name lives under the label acme_service, not service. The working selector is therefore {namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"}. Over the authorized window 2026-11-21T09:59:24Z–2026-11-22T09:59:24Z that stream holds 16 lines in total, split by the parsed level label as ERROR 4, INFO 10, WARN 2; so the answer is 4 error-level lines. All four ERROR lines fall in the 2026-11-22T03:59:24Z–09:59:24Z slice (count for that slice is also 4) and are timestamped 2026-11-22T09:58:49.259101Z to 2026-11-22T09:58:49.259385Z from pod checkout-698c8f5df-2z6dv via job checkout-logs. Their exact messages are: "Payment processor refused: invalid token (txn 9d1f)", "Inventory check timed out for SKU-77481", "Order persistence failed: deadlock on orders table" and "Webhook delivery exhausted retries for partner ACME". This is a log-count reading only: four unrelated-looking error messages do not by themselves establish a cause, and no root-cause object is named.

claims.text: The lines returned for selector {namespace="app-282"} carry exactly the Loki labels acme_service, filename, job, level, namespace and pod (values seen: acme_service=checkout, job=checkout-logs, filename=/var/log/checkout.log, pod=checkout-698c8f5df-2z6dv); no label named service appears in that returned label set, which is why the requested selector name does not match this data.
sum(count_over_time({namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"}[24h])) at 2026-11-22T09:59:24Z returned 16, i.e. 16 log lines from that stream inside the authorized window.

sum by (level) (count_over_time({namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"} | json [24h])) at 2026-11-22T09:59:24Z returned three series: level=ERROR 4, level=INFO 10, level=WARN 2 — four error-level log lines in the authorized window.
The same ERROR count evaluated over the shorter window 2026-11-22T03:59:24Z–09:59:24Z returned 4, so all four error-level lines lie in the last six hours of the authorized window.

Querying {namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"} |= "ERROR" over 2026-11-22T03:59:24Z–09:59:24Z returned exactly 4 lines, all from pod checkout-698c8f5df-2z6dv (job=checkout-logs, level=ERROR) timestamped 2026-11-22T09:58:49.259101Z to 2026-11-22T09:58:49.259385Z, with the messages "Payment processor refused: invalid token (txn 9d1f)", "Inventory check timed out for SKU-77481", "Order persistence failed: deadlock on orders table" and "Webhook delivery exhausted retries for partner ACME".

The narrower window 2026-11-22T07:59:24Z–09:59:24Z returned the same 4 ERROR lines with identical timestamps and messages, confirming the error burst sits in the final minutes before 2026-11-22T09:59:24Z.

Because the four ERROR lines are emitted within about 0.3 ms of one another (2026-11-22T09:58:49.259101Z–.259385Z) immediately after ten "Checkout flow completed for cart N" INFO lines at 2026-11-22T09:58:49.259494Z–.259864Z, they may be a single synthetic error burst in one request cycle rather than four independent failures; the evidence does not establish this and does not show the requests or dependencies behind each message.

Query checkout logs with {namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"} (optionally | json | level="ERROR") rather than {service="checkout"}; the latter matches nothing because the stream carries acme_service, not service.

gaps: The requested query {service="checkout"} (window 2026-11-21T09:59:24Z–2026-11-22T09:59:24Z, limit 50) returned no series (status no_data, 0 lines). That empty result shows only that this query matched nothing in that window and is recorded here as a gap, not as evidence that no label named service exists anywhere in Loki.

Two line-level queries over the full 24-hour window — {namespace="app-282", acme_service="checkout"} | json | level="ERROR" and the same selector with |= "ERROR" — both failed with TOOL_TIMEOUT and returned no content, so the individual error lines were only retrieved from the shorter 6-hour and 2-hour windows; lines from the first 18 hours of the window were not read, and error-level lines there are unknown.

The per-6-hour ERROR count queries for 2026-11-21T09:59:24Z–15:59:24Z, 15:59:24Z–21:59:24Z and 21:59:24Z–03:59:24Z returned no series (status no_data). Absence of a series is not a zero, so error counts for those slices remain unknown from these queries; they cannot be cited either way.

Whether the 4 ERROR messages correspond to real downstream failures (payment processor, inventory, orders persistence, partner webhook) or to injected/fault-configured behavior was not established: no traces, Prometheus series or Kubernetes objects were examined in this Run.
change_history is not an integrated source in this Run, so no deployment, config or fault-injection change could be correlated with the 2026-11-22T09:58:49Z error burst.

Loki counts are limited by retention/ingest and by the label selector; lines not ingested or outside the retained data are unknown, and the stream's pod name (checkout-698c8f5df-2z6dv) was not verified against live Kubernetes objects.
next_steps: If the error burst matters, pull checkout traces and RPC/HTTP error metrics for 2026-11-22T09:58:00Z–10:00:00Z to see which dependency (payment, inventory/orders persistence, webhook partner) failed at that instant.
Re-run the ERROR count on a shorter window per hour (e.g. 1-hour slices) instead of 6-hour slices to get citable per-slice error counts, since the 6-hour no_data results cannot be read as zero.

Check the checkout pod's Kubernetes status, events and previous-container logs for checkout-698c8f5df-2z6dv, and review its ConfigMaps for any fault-injection settings, since a configuration change or injected fault could produce this single-instant error burst.
